Issued at 516 AM CDT Sat Sep 26 2026

A broad, negatively-tilted upper level trough axis extends from
the Canadian Rockies to the Central Plains early this morning. 
Shortwave energy moving poleward has produced a broken area of 
light rain from north central North Dakota through eastern South
Dakota. This rain will continue to lift north/northeastward 
this morning and should shift east of the forecast area by noon.
Another shortwave embedded in the main trough can be seen on 
water vapor imagery ejecting off the Rockies of Montana early 
this morning, and a lee surface trough has already sharpened 
through eastern Montana in response. As had been advertised by 
some high-resolution models, scattered showers and isolated 
thunderstorms are beginning to develop along the ND/MT 
stateline, north of the Missouri River. Model consensus has this
activity gradually dissipating while moving into north central 
North Dakota later this morning. The NAMnest has been an outlier
in simulating strong, if not marginally severe thunderstorms, 
but effective bulk shear around 25 kts and MUCAPE no greater 
than around 1000 J/kg is not really supportive of a severe 
threat. 

The surface lee trough is attendant to a deepening cyclone over
northern Alberta/Saskatchewan and will gain forward momentum 
into western North Dakota as a cold front/dryline as the 
Canadian low becomes stacked and begins occluding this morning 
and afternoon. Gusty west-northwest winds (maximum gusts around 
25-30 mph) are expected behind the front in western North 
Dakota from mid morning to early afternoon, with winds along 
and behind the front trending weaker as it reaches central 
North Dakota. The front is expected to clear persistent low 
clouds, but may not reach the Turtle Mountains through James 
River Valley before peak diurnal heating ceases. The high 
temperature forecast in the mid to upper 60s in these parts of 
the state may be too optimistic if an overcast sky prevails 
through the day. The western half of the state will likely see 
high temperatures around 70 to near 75 this afternoon, warmest 
just ahead of the front during the mid to late afternoon due to
compressional heating. The dry air mass trailing the front is 
expected to bring RH as low as 25 percent in far southwest 
North Dakota during the mid to late afternoon. But because the 
strongest winds are expected to subside by mid afternoon, near- 
critical fire weather conditions are not anticipated. 

A few CAMs want to develop some light showers ahead of the cold
front this evening in the southern James River Valley, but the 
chance for measurable rain is very low. The southern flank of 
the cold front is forecast to stall between Lake Oahe and the 
southern Red River Valley overnight while the northern flank 
surges eastward through the northern Red River Valley. The 
cooler and drier air mass behind the front associated with 
surface high pressure expanding southeastward off the Canadian 
Rockies will allow temperatures to drop into the 40s tonight, 
possibly falling into the upper 30s in low-lying areas across 
the west. There may be just enough of a low level breeze to 
prevent strong radiational cooling from tanking temperatures 
below the 10th percentile of the NBM minimum temperature 
distribution, which is as cold as the mid to upper 30s.

Surface high pressure will slide eastward through the region on
Sunday, keeping winds light for most areas with afternoon highs
in the 60s. By Sunday evening, shortwave energy will begin 
racing from the Great Basin to the Northern Plains ahead of a 
potent trough digging into California. The downstream response 
of increasing low level warm air advection and moisture 
transport lends to increasing chances for showers and 
thunderstorms through Sunday night, with widespread showers and
scattered thunderstorms likely across all but northwest North 
Dakota by Monday morning. That is not to say that there will 
not be any showers or storms in the northwest, but odds are 
lower there (10 to 40 percent chance of rain) than elsewhere 
(70 to 100 percent chance of rain). The initial round of 
showers and storms is forecast to propagate into eastern North 
Dakota Monday afternoon, but the arrival of a northern stream 
wave under a coupled upper level jet could force another batch 
of showers and storms Monday afternoon before the first round 
fully departs. A weak cold front attendant to the northern 
stream wave should push showers and storms off to the southeast
through Monday night. Ensemble guidance continues to hone in on
a corridor from south central North Dakota to northwest 
Minnesota for the highest rain amounts, where the latest NBM 
shows high chances (80 to 95 percent) for exceeding half an 
inch of rain, medium to high chances (60 to 85 percent) for 
exceeding one inch of rain, and low to medium chances (20 to 45
